kjv-isaiah-block-quotation: The Book of Mormon says Lehi's family carried brass plates out of Jerusalem around 600 BC containing the Hebrew scriptures, and quotes long stretches of Isaiah from them. The question is what those quotations look like. They match the King James Version of 1611 — an English translation made more than two thousand years later — word for word, including its distinctive phrasing. A fresh translation from ancient plates would not be expected to land on one particular English edition.
kjv-italics-revision: Open a King James Bible and you will see some words printed in italics. Those are words the 1611 translators added to make the English read smoothly — they are not in the Hebrew or Greek. Nobody translating from ancient plates would know which words those were. So it matters a great deal where the Book of Mormon's Isaiah differs from the KJV: the changes cluster on exactly those italicized words.
kjv-translation-errors-copied: Every translation makes mistakes, and the 1611 King James has a number of known ones — places where later scholarship showed the translators misread the Hebrew. Those errors belong to that English edition; they are not in the underlying ancient text. This case looks at what happens when the Book of Mormon quotes passages containing them, and whether a translation made directly from an older source would reproduce a seventeenth-century mistake.
deutero-isaiah-problem: Most scholars hold that the book of Isaiah had more than one author — chapters 1–39 from the eighth-century prophet, and chapters 40 onward from a writer during the Babylonian exile, which began in 586 BC. Lehi supposedly left Jerusalem around 600 BC, before that. So if the later chapters were written after he left, they could not have been on the plates he took. The Book of Mormon quotes them anyway.
sermon-on-mount-3-nephi: The Book of Mormon has Jesus visit the Americas after his resurrection and preach a version of the Sermon on the Mount. Because we have thousands of Greek manuscripts of Matthew, scholars can trace how the wording changed over centuries of copying. This case asks which stage of that history the Nephite version matches — the earliest manuscripts, or the later medieval family of copies the King James translators happened to use.
nt-phrasing-in-preexilic-books: The earliest parts of the Book of Mormon are set around 600 BC, six centuries before the New Testament was written. Yet distinctive New Testament phrases — wording that first appears in Paul's letters or in John — show up in those sections. This case is about what that repetition suggests: an ancient Hebrew record that happens to anticipate Greek Christian vocabulary, or a nineteenth-century writer steeped in the King James Bible.
hebrews-in-alma-12-13: Alma 12–13 discusses the priesthood of Melchizedek — a shadowy figure mentioned twice in the Hebrew Bible and developed at length in the New Testament letter to the Hebrews. The Alma passage is set around 82 BC, long before Hebrews was written. This case compares the two side by side, looking at whether Alma simply shares a theme with Hebrews or follows its specific argument and sequence.
mark-long-ending-mormon-9: The Gospel of Mark has a well-known textual problem: the oldest and best manuscripts end at 16:8, and verses 9–20 are missing from them. Most modern Bibles footnote this. Those disputed verses are almost certainly a later addition. The Book of Mormon quotes from them — which raises the question of how a passage added to Mark centuries after Christ ended up in a record buried in the Americas.
horses-anachronism: The Book of Mormon mentions horses in the Americas repeatedly, and in some passages chariots. The problem is chronological: horses evolved in North America but went extinct there thousands of years before the Book of Mormon's timeline, and were reintroduced by Spanish colonists after 1492. No horse remains from the relevant period have been found. This is one of a cluster of animals, plants and metals that raise the same question.
steel-and-ferrous-metallurgy: Nephi says he made a bow of 'fine steel,' and swords of steel appear later. Steel is iron deliberately alloyed with carbon and worked at high temperature, and it leaves distinctive archaeological traces — furnaces, slag, tools. No iron or steel industry has been found in the pre-Columbian Americas of that era. Defenders argue 'steel' could be loose language for another hard metal, which this case examines.
wheat-barley-silk: The Book of Mormon lists wheat and barley among Nephite crops and mentions silk among their fabrics. All three are Old World products: wheat and barley were domesticated in the Near East, and silk comes from a moth cultivated in China. None has been found in pre-Columbian American archaeology. The question is whether these are translation approximations for local products, or whether they belong to the world the writer knew.
greek-names-timothy-lachoneus: Lehi's family leaves Jerusalem in 600 BC speaking Hebrew and writing in a form of Egyptian, and never has contact with Greece. Yet Greek names appear among their descendants — Timothy, Lachoneus — and so does an expression built on the Greek alphabet ('alpha and omega'). This case is about how Greek got into an isolated Hebrew colony centuries before Alexander made Greek an international language.
church-bible-synagogue-terms: Words carry their history. 'Church' translates a Greek word for a called-out assembly and belongs to the Christian era. 'Synagogue' is Greek and describes an institution that developed among Jews later than 600 BC. 'Bible' comes from Greek for 'the books' and names a collection that did not exist yet. All three appear in the Book of Mormon's earliest sections, which this case examines as a set.
another-gospel-canon-closure: Two verses get used constantly against the Book of Mormon: Galatians 1:8, where Paul condemns 'any other gospel,' and Revelation 22:18, which warns against adding to 'this book.' This case is unusual on this site because it takes the Christian side of the argument apart first. Revelation 22 is about the book of Revelation, not a Bible that did not yet exist as a collection — and saying otherwise is bad reading.
grace-after-all-we-can-do: 2 Nephi 25:23 says we are saved by grace 'after all we can do.' That phrase is the heart of a long argument, because it seems to attach a condition to grace: your own maximum effort first, then God makes up the difference. Paul writes in Ephesians 2 that salvation is a gift 'not of works, lest any man should boast.' This case sets the two statements beside each other and examines both readings.
dark-skin-curse: Several Book of Mormon passages describe God cursing the Lamanites with a 'skin of blackness' as a mark of their rebellion, and describe righteous Lamanites becoming 'white and delightsome.' In 1981 the church changed 'white' to 'pure' in one verse, and in 2010 revised the chapter headings that had spelled the doctrine out. This case walks through what the text says, what the church taught, and what has since been edited.
fortunate-fall: In the Book of Mormon, 2 Nephi 2:25 says 'Adam fell that men might be; and men are, that they might have joy.' The Fall becomes a necessary and even good step — without it there would be no human family and no path to joy. Historic Christianity has read the Fall as catastrophe: the entry of sin and death that Christ came to reverse. This case examines a genuine difference in what the story means.
original-sin-infant-baptism: Moroni 8 addresses whether babies should be baptized, and answers with unusual force: infant baptism is 'solemn mockery,' and anyone who supposes little children need it is 'in the gall of bitterness' and in danger of hell. That is a strong condemnation of a practice most of the Christian world has followed for centuries. This case examines both the doctrine of original sin behind the dispute and the severity of the language.
trinitarian-monotheism-1830: The Book of Mormon speaks of God in terms that sound like one God in three persons — the Father, the Son and the Holy Ghost as 'one God, without end.' Later LDS teaching describes three separate beings and holds that faithful humans can become gods themselves. This case examines the gap between the 1830 book and the doctrine that developed afterwards, using the church's own texts on both ends.
1837-son-of-edits: In 1830 the Book of Mormon called Mary 'the mother of God' and said an angel had shown Nephi 'the Eternal Father.' In the 1837 edition several of those phrases gained the words 'the Son of' — 'the mother of the Son of God,' 'the Son of the Eternal Father.' This case examines the changes themselves and what they suggest about how the doctrine of God developed.
jacob-polygamy-vs-dc132: Jacob 2 is one of the sharpest passages in the Book of Mormon: taking multiple wives is 'abominable' before God, and the Lord says he has heard the mourning of the daughters of his people. Thirteen years later Joseph Smith recorded D&C 132, which commands plural marriage. This case sets the two documents beside each other — and notes that the Bible agrees with the Book of Mormon here.
unchangeable-god-vs-king-follett: Moroni 8:18 says God is 'unchangeable from all eternity to all eternity.' In 1844, at a funeral for a man named King Follett, Joseph Smith preached that God 'was once as we are now' — an exalted man who progressed to godhood. Those two statements are hard to hold together, and this case examines whether the later teaching develops the earlier one or contradicts it.
no-postmortem-repentance: Alma 34:32–35 is emphatic: this life is the time to prepare to meet God, and there is no labour performed after death. Later LDS teaching added the spirit world, where the gospel is preached to the dead, and proxy baptism — living members baptized on behalf of the deceased. This case examines whether that development fits the Book of Mormon's own warning or reverses it.
born-at-jerusalem: Alma 7:10 prophesies that Jesus will be born 'at Jerusalem, which is the land of our forefathers.' Micah 5:2 names Bethlehem, and Matthew and Luke both place the birth there. Defenders argue that 'at Jerusalem' means the surrounding region, which is a real usage in ancient texts. This case examines that defense alongside how the Book of Mormon uses place-names elsewhere.
plain-precious-things-removed: 1 Nephi 13 describes a 'great and abominable church' removing 'many plain and precious things' from the Bible before it reached the nations. That claim is what makes a restored scripture necessary. It is also testable, because we have thousands of manuscripts from before and across that period. This case examines what the manuscript record actually shows about large-scale removal.
no-nephite-material-culture: The Book of Mormon describes cities, temples, roads, coinage, metal armour and wars involving hundreds of thousands. Civilizations of that size leave debris — pottery, foundations, weapons, burials — and American archaeology has excavated extensively. No site has ever been identified with a Book of Mormon city, and the church takes no official position on where any of it happened. This case examines the state of the evidence and the main LDS responses.
no-semitic-inscriptions: Writing is durable. Egyptian and Hebrew inscriptions survive across the Old World in stone, clay and metal. The Book of Mormon describes a literate people keeping records for a thousand years in 'reformed Egyptian.' No pre-Columbian inscription in Hebrew, Egyptian or any related script has ever been authenticated in the Americas — and 'reformed Egyptian' is a term unknown to Egyptology.
dna-native-american-origins: The Book of Mormon presents Lehi's family as ancestors of Native Americans, and the church's own introduction called the Lamanites 'the principal ancestors of the American Indians' until 2006, when it was changed to 'among the ancestors.' Population genetics consistently traces Native American ancestry to northeast Asia. This case examines both the science and the church's own quiet revision of its introduction.
population-growth-impossible: The Book of Mormon starts with one family — a few dozen people — and within a few centuries describes armies in the tens of thousands and a final battle with hundreds of thousands of dead. Demographers can model population growth from a founding group. This case works through whether the numbers are reachable at any realistic birth rate, and looks at the main proposed solution, which is that other people were already there.
translation-seer-stone: For about 150 years, church manuals and paintings showed Joseph Smith reading from the gold plates. What the eyewitness accounts describe is different: he put a brown stone he had earlier used for treasure-hunting into his hat, buried his face in it to block the light, and dictated — often with the plates covered or not in the room. The church published photographs of the stone and confirmed the method in 2015.
lost-116-pages: Joseph Smith's scribe Martin Harris borrowed the first 116 pages of the translation and lost them. Retranslating the same text would have produced a comparable document, and anyone holding the pages could have compared them. Instead a revelation instructed that a different set of plates covering the same period be translated. This case examines that solution and what it implies about the translation process.
witnesses-character-and-vision: Eleven men signed statements printed in the front of every Book of Mormon about seeing the plates, and their testimony is one of the strongest arguments for it. This case takes it seriously and looks closely: the language several of them used later — 'spiritual eyes,' 'the eye of faith' — the fact that all three of the Three Witnesses left the church, and their involvement in other visionary movements.
gold-plates-never-examined: The plates were reportedly returned to the angel Moroni after the translation, so no historian, metallurgist or independent witness ever examined them. That is not by itself proof of anything — many ancient artifacts are lost. But it does mean the central physical evidence for the Book of Mormon is permanently unavailable for testing, which is worth stating plainly and weighing.
kinderhook-plates: In 1843 some men near Kinderhook, Illinois, produced six small brass plates covered in strange characters. Joseph Smith reportedly began translating them, identifying a descendant of Ham. The plates were a deliberate hoax, and one of the makers later admitted it; metallurgical testing in 1980 confirmed a nineteenth-century origin. This case examines what he said, how firmly it can be sourced, and what it shows about his method.
source-parallels-voth-late-war: Two books published before 1830 keep coming up: Ethan Smith's View of the Hebrews (1823), which argued Native Americans descend from the lost tribes of Israel, and Gilbert Hunt's The Late War (1816), which narrated the War of 1812 in King James English. Both were available in Joseph Smith's region. This case examines how strong the parallels really are, in both directions.
book-of-abraham-papyri: This is the one case where the source document survives. In 1835 Joseph Smith bought Egyptian papyri from a travelling mummy exhibition and said they contained a lost record of Abraham; he published the Book of Abraham from them. The papyri were thought destroyed but fragments resurfaced in 1966. Every Egyptologist who has examined them — including LDS scholars — identifies them as ordinary funerary texts with no connection to Abraham.
stylometry-wordprint-studies: Writers have measurable habits — how often they use small function words — and statisticians have tried to use those fingerprints to identify who wrote the Book of Mormon. One study pointed to Sidney Rigdon and Solomon Spalding; BYU studies concluded the book has multiple distinct authorial voices. This case examines both, and is honest that the method is contested enough that neither settles the question.
jst-genesis-50-choice-seer: Joseph Smith produced a revised Bible, and in his version of Genesis 50 the dying Joseph of Egypt prophesies a future 'choice seer' who will be named Joseph, as his father was. No ancient manuscript of Genesis contains this passage — not the Hebrew, not the Dead Sea Scrolls, not the Greek. This case examines a prophecy of the translator, inserted into the text by the translator.
angel-nephi-moroni-name-change: Every Latter-day Saint knows the angel who appeared to Joseph Smith in 1823 as Moroni. But the 1842 Times and Seasons account, published under his own editorship, and the 1851 Pearl of Great Price both name the angel Nephi. The name was later corrected. This case examines the documents and the explanations offered — a scribal slip, or a detail that changed.
first-vision-multiple-accounts: The First Vision is the founding event of the church: God the Father and Jesus Christ appearing to Joseph Smith in a grove of trees. He told it more than once, and the accounts differ — in the year, in his age, in whether one being appeared or two, and in what he was seeking. The church published an essay acknowledging this in 2013. This case sets the four firsthand accounts side by side.
first-vision-revival-dating: The 1838 account, the one in scripture, sets the vision during an intense religious revival in Palmyra in 1820 that stirred up the whole neighbourhood. Historians have gone looking for that revival in newspapers, church minutes and membership records. What the record shows is a major revival in the area in 1824–25 — after the date given — and this case examines the evidence and the proposed reconciliations.
quitmormon-resignation-difficulty: Leaving most churches means simply not going. Formally removing your name from LDS records has historically required a letter, sometimes an interview, and follow-up contact from local leaders. The process was burdensome enough that a lawyer set up a free service to handle it, and more than 150,000 people have used it. This case is about what that volume indicates rather than about any individual's experience.
temple-wedding-family-exclusion: LDS temple marriages are performed inside the temple, and only members holding a current temple recommend may enter. That means a parent who is not a member, or who is a member but does not hold a recommend — including for not paying a full tithe — waits outside during their own child's wedding. This case examines the practice, the reasoning behind it, and the policy changes made in 2019.
byu-honor-code-disaffiliation: Brigham Young University is owned by the church, and its honor code requires students to remain in good standing with it. A student who formally resigns membership loses eligibility to continue — not for misconduct, but for changing their mind. This case examines the policy as written, including how it applies differently to students who were never members in the first place.
social-costs-shunning: The LDS Church does not have a formal shunning policy, and officially discourages cutting off family members who leave — a genuine difference from some other groups examined on this site. The costs are nonetheless real and documented: strained families, lost friendships, exclusion from temple weddings, and in Utah communities the loss of an entire social world. This case tries to describe them accurately without overstating them.
grenfell-exit-testimony: Alyssa Grenfell is a former Latter-day Saint who has written and spoken publicly about leaving. This case uses her account as a specific, checkable window into what the exit involves — the temple garments, the contact from leaders afterwards, and the long process of rethinking a worldview. Personal testimony is not proof of doctrine; it is evidence about experience, and it is treated that way here.
ces-letter-gospel-topics-visibility: In 2013 Jeremy Runnells wrote an open letter listing historical problems as questions to a Church Educational System director. It spread widely online, and many members encountered this material for the first time. Between 2013 and 2015 the church published thirteen unsigned essays conceding much of it — originally without links from the main site navigation. This case examines both the letter and how the response was rolled out.
september-six: In September 1993 the church disciplined six scholars and writers in quick succession — excommunicating five and disfellowshipping one. They included historians working on church history and writers on feminist theology. This case examines what each had published, what the discipline was for, and what the coordinated timing suggests about the boundaries of permitted inquiry.
sec-ensign-peak-settlement: In 2023 the US Securities and Exchange Commission fined the church and its investment arm, Ensign Peak Advisors, a total of $5 million. The finding was that for roughly two decades the size of its portfolio had been obscured by filing through more than a dozen shell companies. This case works from the SEC's own order and the church's response.
nephite-non-levite-priesthood: The law of Moses restricts priesthood and sacrifice to the tribe of Levi, and specifically to Aaron's descendants. Lehi's family descends from Joseph, not Levi. Yet the Book of Mormon has Nephites building temples, consecrating priests and offering sacrifices while claiming to keep the law of Moses. This case examines the tension and the explanations offered for it.
temples-outside-jerusalem: Deuteronomy 12 is emphatic that Israel must offer sacrifice at one place that God chooses, not wherever they please — the reasoning behind the centrality of the Jerusalem temple. The Book of Mormon has Nephi build a temple 'after the manner of Solomon's' in the Americas, and others follow. This case examines whether faithful Israelites in exile could have done that under the law they claimed to keep.
christ-remains-in-heaven-acts-3: Acts 3:21 says heaven 'must receive' Christ until the restoration of all things — which reads as a statement that he remains there until his final return. The Book of Mormon has him descend and minister in the Americas shortly after the resurrection. This case examines whether the two can be reconciled, including the argument that the ascension in Acts 1 comes after the Nephite visit.
joseph-smith-failed-prophecies: Deuteronomy 18:22 gives a simple public test for anyone claiming to speak for God: if the thing predicted does not happen, the LORD did not say it. Joseph Smith made a number of dated, checkable predictions — a temple built in Independence within that generation, the success of the Kirtland bank, and others. This case lays them out against that standard, including the defenses offered for each.
word-of-wisdom-dietary-law: D&C 89, given in 1833, advises against alcohol, tobacco, and 'hot drinks' — later interpreted as coffee and tea — and was explicitly given 'not by commandment.' Under Heber J. Grant in the 1920s, keeping it became a requirement for temple entry. This case examines the shift from counsel to requirement, and the New Testament passages that address making food rules a test of fellowship.
temple-garments-practice: Members who have received the temple endowment wear a prescribed two-piece undergarment day and night, and it is treated as sacred rather than secret. Compliance is asked about in temple recommend interviews. This case describes the practice accurately — which most outside accounts do not — and examines the biblical question of prescribing sacred clothing for ordinary daily life.
exaltation-eternal-progression: Exaltation is the highest LDS destiny: a faithful couple, sealed in the temple, becomes gods with eternal increase and worlds of their own. It is the reason the temple exists. Against it stand Isaiah's flat statements — 'before me there was no God formed, neither shall there be after me' — which this case sets alongside the LDS sources describing the doctrine.
priesthood-temple-ban-1852-1978: From 1852 until 1978, Black members of the LDS Church could not hold the priesthood — which almost all other men received at twelve — or enter the temple. Church leaders defended it in print with explanations about premortal conduct and the curse of Cain. In 1978 it was lifted by revelation, and in 2013 the church formally disavowed the old explanations. This case works from those sources.
endowment-masonic-origins: Joseph Smith was initiated as a Freemason in March 1842. Seven weeks later he introduced the temple endowment, which included handclasps, signs, tokens, penalty gestures and an oath of secrecy that closely resembled Masonic ritual. The penalty gestures were removed in 1990. This case examines the parallels and the main LDS explanation — that Masonry preserves a corrupted fragment of an ancient original.
heavenly-mother-doctrine: LDS teaching holds that everyone existed as a spirit child of Heavenly Parents before birth — a Heavenly Father and a Heavenly Mother. The doctrine is affirmed officially, though members have been discouraged from praying to her or speculating publicly. This case examines the teaching and the fact that the Bible, across both Testaments, never mentions a divine mother.
jesus-firstborn-spirit-attained-godhood: In LDS theology Jesus is the firstborn spirit child of Heavenly Parents — the eldest of a family that includes every human being — who then progressed to godhood. Historic Christianity holds that the Son is eternal and uncreated, of the same being as the Father. This case examines the difference, which is larger than it first appears and touches everything downstream.
jesus-lucifer-spirit-brothers: Because LDS theology makes all spirits children of Heavenly Parents, Jesus and Lucifer are both in that family, and Latter-day Saints have taught that they are spirit brothers. Members often find the phrasing jarring when outsiders use it, so this case is careful to state the doctrine as the church states it before examining what it implies about the nature of Christ.
god-exalted-man-flesh-and-bone: D&C 130:22 says the Father has 'a body of flesh and bones as tangible as man's,' and the King Follett discourse teaches that God was once a man who progressed to godhood. Historic Christianity holds that God is spirit and has always been God. This case examines the LDS sources, and the biblical statements — John 4:24, Numbers 23:19, Psalm 90:2 — that stand against them.
different-jesus-hinckley-1998: In 1998 church president Gordon B. Hinckley was asked whether the LDS Jesus is the same as the traditional Christian Jesus, and answered that 'the traditional Christ of whom I speak is not the Christ of whom I speak.' The remark is quoted constantly, so this case gives the full context and asks the fair question: how much difference makes a different Jesus?
premortal-spirit-children: LDS doctrine teaches that before birth every human lived as a spirit child in the presence of Heavenly Parents, chose to accept the plan of salvation, and came to earth to gain a body. It explains a great deal about why LDS members see life as they do. This case examines the teaching and the biblical texts on both sides, including Jeremiah 1:5, which is the passage most often cited for it.
trinity-vs-godhead: Historic Christianity confesses one God in three persons — Father, Son and Holy Spirit sharing one being. LDS teaching describes the Godhead as three separate beings perfectly united in purpose. Both sides can accuse the other of misrepresenting them, so this case states each position in its own words first, then examines which the biblical texts support.
blood-atonement: Brigham Young and other nineteenth-century leaders taught that some sins were so serious that Christ's atonement could not cover them, and that the sinner's own blood had to be shed for their salvation. The church has repudiated the doctrine and denies it was ever practised. This case works from the recorded sermons themselves, and is careful about the difference between what was taught and what was done.
js-polygamy-wives-count-ages: The church's own Gospel Topics essay states that Joseph Smith had between thirty and forty wives, that the youngest was Helen Mar Kimball at fourteen, and that some were already married to other men. For most of the twentieth century this was denied or minimized. This case works entirely from the church's own published sources and the Joseph Smith Papers.
js-polyandry: At least ten of Joseph Smith's plural wives were already married to living husbands, some of whom were away on missions. This practice — a woman sealed to two men at once — is called polyandry, and it is the hardest part of the record to explain even for defenders. This case examines the documented cases and the main explanations offered, including that some sealings were 'eternity only.'
dc132-emma-destroyed: D&C 132 is the revelation commanding plural marriage, and it is addressed in part to Joseph Smith's wife Emma. Verse 54 warns that if she does not accept it, she will be destroyed. This case reads the section as it stands in LDS scripture today and examines what kind of revelation contains a threat to a specific named person who is resisting it.
js-polygamy-denials: While married to more than thirty women, Joseph Smith publicly denied practising polygamy — including a statement in 1844 that he had only one wife. Defenders point to the legal and physical danger the practice created, and to the church's later admission that secrecy was necessary. This case sets the public statements beside the sealing records and examines both.
eternal-polygamy-today: The LDS Church stopped performing plural marriages in 1890, and members who practise polygamy today are excommunicated. But the doctrine of eternal plural marriage remains: a widowed man may be sealed to a second wife while remaining sealed to the first, and a woman may not. This case examines the current practice, which surprises many members and most outsiders.
mountain-meadows-massacre: In September 1857 a wagon train of emigrants travelling through southern Utah was besieged, offered safe passage under a white flag, and then killed — about 120 men, women and children, with only the youngest spared. The attackers were a local Mormon militia, with some Paiute involvement. This case examines the event, the long dispute over who authorized it, and the church's own historians' findings.
nauvoo-expositor-carthage: Joseph Smith is remembered as a martyr, killed by a mob at Carthage Jail in 1844. The events leading there are less often told: a newspaper, the Nauvoo Expositor, published one issue exposing plural marriage; as mayor, Smith had the press destroyed; that led to his arrest. He also had a smuggled pistol and fired it. This case fills in the sequence without diminishing the killing.
oath-of-vengeance: From about 1845 until 1927, the temple endowment included an oath in which participants prayed that God would avenge the blood of the prophets on this nation. It was added after Joseph Smith's killing and removed in the 1920s amid political scrutiny. This case examines the wording and its history, and is careful to note that it is not part of the ceremony today.
danites-1838: In Missouri in 1838, amid genuine and severe persecution of the Latter-day Saints, a secret band called the Danites formed among them and carried out raids and intimidation. Their existence is not disputed by anyone. What is argued about is how much Joseph Smith knew and approved, which this case examines from the sources on both sides — including the persecution that preceded it.
policy-of-exclusion-2015: In November 2015 a leaked handbook change barred children living with a same-sex parent from baptism until they turned eighteen and disavowed such relationships, and classified those relationships as apostasy. Church president Russell M. Nelson later described the policy as revelation. In April 2019 it was reversed. This case examines a policy called revelation, reversed within four years.
tithing-enforcement: Latter-day Saints are asked whether they pay a full tithe in the interview required for a temple recommend, and a negative answer means no recommend — which means no temple attendance and no attending a child's temple wedding. This case examines that link between a financial commitment and access to family events, and the biblical teaching on giving that stands beside it.
missionary-program-realities: Around 70,000 young Latter-day Saints serve missions at any time. They are unpaid, funded by their own families, assigned a companion they are rarely alone from, and — until recent changes — could call home only twice a year. This case describes the structure accurately and examines what that degree of control means, including the real formative benefits many missionaries describe.
prophetic-fallibility-unfalsifiable: Church leaders have taught that the prophet 'will never lead the church astray.' Leaders have also taught things later abandoned — Adam-God, blood atonement, the racial priesthood ban's justifications — which are now attributed to the limitations of the men rather than to revelation. This case examines whether a claim that can absorb any outcome is still a claim that can be tested.
abuse-helpline-2022: The church operates a help line that local lay bishops must call when abuse is disclosed. A 2022 Associated Press investigation into a case in Bisbee, Arizona, reported that the line routed bishops to church attorneys and that abuse continued for years without a report to authorities. The church disputes the characterization. This case examines the reporting, the church's response, and the clergy-privilege law involved.
kirtland-safety-society: In 1836 the church established a bank in Kirtland, Ohio. It was denied a charter, operated anyway, issued notes, and collapsed within months, wiping out members' savings. Joseph Smith had encouraged investment and was fined for illegal banking. Roughly a third of church leadership left over it. This case examines the episode and the claim of revelation attached to it.
post-manifesto-polygamy: The 1890 Manifesto is presented as the end of plural marriage. In fact new plural marriages continued to be performed — in Mexico, Canada and at sea — with the knowledge of church leaders, for another fourteen years, until a Second Manifesto in 1904 and the excommunication of two apostles. This case examines the gap between the public statement and the private practice.
facsimile-1-lion-couch: The Book of Abraham prints three Egyptian illustrations with Joseph Smith's explanations, and this is the first: a figure on a couch, which he identified as Abraham about to be sacrificed by a pagan priest. Egyptologists identify the same scene type immediately — it is a standard embalming or resurrection vignette, with Anubis attending Osiris. This case compares the two readings figure by figure.
facsimile-2-hypocephalus: The second facsimile is a hypocephalus, a disc placed under a mummy's head. Joseph Smith's explanation of Figure 7 calls it 'God sitting upon his throne, revealing through the heavens the grand key-words of the priesthood.' Egyptologists identify the figure as Min, an ithyphallic fertility god. This case sets the labels against the standard readings, which can be checked in any Egyptological reference.
facsimile-3-presentation: The third facsimile is the most testable of the three, because it contains readable Egyptian captions naming the figures. Joseph Smith identified them as Abraham on Pharaoh's throne, a prince, and a king. The captions themselves name Osiris, Isis, Maat and an offering-bearer — and identify as women two figures he labelled as men. This case simply reads what the inscriptions say.
adam-god-doctrine: Brigham Young taught repeatedly from the pulpit, and later in the temple, that Adam 'is our Father and our God, and the only God with whom we have to do.' The teaching was published in the Journal of Discourses. In 1976 Spencer W. Kimball denounced it as false doctrine. This case examines what it means for a prophet to have taught error from the pulpit for decades.
priesthood-restoration-late-account: The restoration of the priesthood by John the Baptist and by Peter, James and John is foundational to LDS authority. What the documents show is that no account of an angelic ordination appears until 1834–35 — several years after the events are dated, and after the church had already been organized. This case examines the documentary timeline and the explanations for the silence.
book-of-commandments-revisions: Joseph Smith's revelations were first published in 1833 as the Book of Commandments. When they were republished in 1835 as the Doctrine and Covenants, many had been revised — with added text, changed wording, and in some places new doctrine. This case compares the two editions on specific sections and asks what it means to edit a document received as the words of God.
egyptian-alphabet-grammar: Alongside the Book of Abraham, Joseph Smith and his scribes produced a document called the Grammar and Alphabet of the Egyptian Language, which assigns meanings to Egyptian characters. It survives, and it is now published by the church in the Joseph Smith Papers. This case examines it as evidence of method: it shows how a single character was expanded into whole paragraphs of English.
zelph-white-lamanite: During the 1834 Zion's Camp march, a skeleton was uncovered on a mound in Illinois. Joseph Smith identified the man as Zelph, a 'white Lamanite' warrior who served under a prophet named Onandagus, and gave details about how he died. The episode is recorded in several participants' journals. This case examines it as a checkable statement about Book of Mormon geography and peoples.
bom-geography-retreat: For over a century, church leaders taught that the Book of Mormon happened across North and South America — Cumorah in New York, Lamanites as the American Indians. As archaeology failed to cooperate, LDS scholarship narrowed the setting to a limited region in Central America, and the church now takes no official position on geography. This case traces that retreat using the church's own statements.
polygamy-coercion-angel-sword: Several women recorded that Joseph Smith told them an angel with a drawn sword had commanded him to take plural wives and would destroy him if he refused — and that accepting would secure their family's salvation. Some were teenagers, and some were told they had a short time to decide. This case examines those accounts, which come largely from the women themselves.
holocaust-proxy-baptisms: Latter-day Saints perform baptisms in temples on behalf of the dead. Jewish groups objected when Holocaust victims began appearing in the records, and the church signed agreements in 1995 and 2010 to stop. Names have continued to appear since — including, at times, prominent ones. This case examines the practice, the agreements, and the church's stated enforcement difficulties.
prop-8-campaign: In 2008 the LDS Church asked California members to volunteer and donate for Proposition 8, a ballot measure defining marriage as between a man and a woman. Members supplied a large share of the campaign's volunteers and donations. This case examines the church's own directives and the later fair-political-practices findings about disclosure, without arguing the merits of the measure itself.
huntsman-tithing-lawsuit: James Huntsman, from a prominent LDS family, sued the church claiming that tithing funds had been used to build the City Creek shopping mall after leaders said no tithing would be used. The case moved through the federal courts with rulings in both directions. This case examines the accounting question at its centre — whether investment returns on tithing are still tithing.
paul-h-dunn-fabrications: Paul H. Dunn was one of the most beloved General Authorities of the 1970s and 80s, famous for gripping stories about professional baseball and combat in the Second World War. Investigation showed many were fabricated or heavily embellished. He admitted it and was given emeritus status. This case examines what happened, and how long the stories circulated as faith-promoting material.
hofmann-forgeries-church-response: In the 1980s Mark Hofmann forged early Mormon documents — including the notorious 'Salamander Letter' — and sold them to the church and to collectors. Church leaders, who claim the gift of discernment, purchased them and in some cases kept them from public view. Hofmann eventually murdered two people with pipe bombs. This case examines the forgeries and the response to them.
burning-in-bosom-epistemology: Moroni 10:4 invites the reader to ask God whether the Book of Mormon is true and promises the Holy Ghost will confirm it; D&C 9 describes a burning in the bosom. This is how most Latter-day Saints know what they know. This case examines that method respectfully and sets it beside the tests the Bible gives — the Bereans checking the scriptures, and the warning to test the spirits.
chiasmus-alma-36: Chiasmus is a mirror-image literary structure (A-B-C-B-A) found throughout Hebrew scripture. In 1967 an LDS scholar showed that Alma 36 is an elaborate chiasm, and it has been the strongest literary argument for ancient authorship ever since. This case takes it seriously and examines the counter-evidence: chiasmus appears in nineteenth-century writing too, and the identification involves judgment calls.
nahom-nhm-altars: This is the strongest archaeological argument for the Book of Mormon, and it deserves a fair hearing. 1 Nephi names a place called Nahom where Ishmael was buried, on the route through Arabia. Altars discovered in Yemen bearing the tribal name NHM date to roughly the right period and sit in roughly the right place. This case examines both what that establishes and what it does not.
succession-crisis: When Joseph Smith was killed in 1844 he left no undisputed successor, and the church fractured. Brigham Young led the largest group west. Smith's widow Emma stayed behind, and his son led what became the Community of Christ. Several of the original witnesses did not follow Young either. This case examines the split and what each group claimed as its authority.
second-anointing: Above the temple endowment sits a rarely-discussed higher ordinance, the second anointing, in which a couple's exaltation is made sure in this life. It is administered by invitation from an apostle, is not mentioned in church curriculum, and most members do not know it exists. This case examines what is known about it and why a hidden top tier matters.
jst-whole-bible: Joseph Smith produced a revision of the entire Bible, correcting what he said had been lost or corrupted. It is a substantial work — thousands of changes, including whole added passages. What is striking is what happened next: the LDS Church has never adopted it as its Bible, and still uses the King James Version. This case examines that decision and what it implies.
lectures-on-faith-decanonized: The Lectures on Faith were published as part of the Doctrine and Covenants in 1835 — the 'doctrine' half of the title — and taught, among other things, that the Father is a personage of spirit. In 1921 they were quietly removed from LDS scripture without a vote of the membership. This case examines the removal and the doctrinal drift behind it.
independence-temple-lot-ownership: In 1832 Joseph Smith prophesied that a temple would be built in Independence, Missouri, 'in this generation.' The generation passed. The specific lot is owned today by the Church of Christ (Temple Lot), a group of a few thousand members, and no temple stands on it. This case examines the prophecy, its wording, and the ways it has been reinterpreted.
zions-camp-dc105-reversal: In 1834 Joseph Smith led an armed march called Zion's Camp to reclaim church lands in Missouri, on the strength of a canonized promise that Zion would be redeemed. The march achieved nothing, cholera killed a number of participants, and a new revelation — D&C 105 — explained that the redemption would wait. This case examines a canonized promise and its canonized walk-back.
one-mighty-and-strong: D&C 85 speaks of 'one mighty and strong' who will set the house of God in order. Because the passage is canonized and vague, it has been claimed by a long series of men announcing themselves as its fulfilment, some of whom founded splinter groups. This case examines the text and the pattern of prophetic claims it keeps generating.
lorenzo-snow-couplet-status: 'As man now is, God once was; as God now is, man may be.' Lorenzo Snow's couplet has been taught for 150 years and summarizes the LDS doctrine of exaltation. In 1997 Gordon B. Hinckley told Time that he did not know that the church teaches it and that not much is known about it. This case examines the couplet's status and that answer.
evolution-shifting-statements: Church leaders have taken strong and opposing positions on evolution — Joseph Fielding Smith rejecting it outright, others accepting it — and BYU teaches it in its biology department. The church's official position today is that it takes no position. This case examines the contradictions in the record rather than the science, because the question here is about prophetic authority.
mormon-name-reversal: In 1990 Gordon B. Hinckley said 'Mormon' should be a badge of honour, and the church ran the 'I'm a Mormon' campaign and owns mormon.org. In 2018 Russell M. Nelson said using the nickname is 'a major victory for Satan.' This case examines the reversal and what it shows about how church statements are received and revised.
avoid-worship-joseph-smith: This is one of the most common Christian misstatements about Latter-day Saints, and it is simply false. Latter-day Saints honour Joseph Smith as a prophet; they do not worship him, they pray to the Father in the name of Jesus, and any member will correct you instantly. This case exists because saying it costs you the conversation and everything true you were about to say.
avoid-coca-cola-ownership: The claim that the church owns Coca-Cola or Pepsi circulates widely, usually as an accusation of hypocrisy about caffeine. It is not true. The church's investment holdings are substantial and were the subject of a real SEC finding — which is a far better argument, and a documented one. This case explains why to drop the rumour and use the fact.
avoid-magic-underwear-mockery: Temple garments are real, and the practice of prescribing sacred clothing is a fair subject for discussion. Calling them 'magic underwear' is not a discussion — it is mockery of something a Latter-day Saint regards as sacred and personal, and it ends conversations instantly. This case explains the practice accurately and shows how to raise it without contempt.
avoid-87-wives-overclaim: Joseph Smith's plural marriages are documented, difficult, and conceded by the church itself: thirty to forty wives, the youngest fourteen, some already married. Inflated numbers circulate — 87 is a common one — and using them lets a defender correct you on a detail and dismiss the whole subject. This case explains why the true number is more than enough.
avoid-mainstream-polygamy-today: The LDS Church stopped performing plural marriages in 1890 and excommunicates members who practise it. Polygamous groups in Utah and Arizona are separate organizations, and Latter-day Saints find being confused with them genuinely offensive. There is a real doctrinal point about eternal plural marriage, which this case explains — but the popular version is wrong.
avoid-white-horse-prophecy: The White Horse Prophecy holds that Latter-day Saints will save the US Constitution when it hangs by a thread. It is not canonized, its text comes from a much later recollection, and church leaders including Joseph F. Smith have publicly rejected it. This case explains why presenting it as LDS doctrine is an error that a knowledgeable member will correct immediately.
avoid-caffeine-ban: The Word of Wisdom forbids 'hot drinks,' interpreted as coffee and tea. Caffeine as such is not prohibited, the church clarified this publicly in 2012, and caffeinated soft drinks are sold on BYU campus. This case exists because the caffeine claim is the fastest way to signal that you do not actually know what Latter-day Saints believe.
avoid-own-planet: The doctrine of exaltation does involve becoming gods with eternal increase, and it is a genuine and serious difference from historic Christianity. But 'you get your own planet' is a caricature that Latter-day Saints do not recognize and church leaders have publicly rejected as a distortion. This case shows how to raise the real doctrine, in LDS language, so it cannot be waved away.
avoid-1826-convicted-conman: In 1826 Joseph Smith appeared before a court in Bainbridge, New York, in connection with treasure-seeking. What the surviving records show is disputed among historians, including whether there was a conviction at all. The episode is genuinely relevant to how he used a seer stone, which this case covers — but the flat claim that he was a convicted fraudster overstates a contested record.
